probe: a package manager this collector can read answers here: an activated Nix system closure, dpkg-query, or rpm. Which one it is comes back in the reason, because it is also the Manager fact every row carries — a host with a manager and nothing installed still answers yes, since zero packages is a reading and not an inability.

collections.name: packages
collections.question: what is installed on this machine, and which package manager says so?

Name.sentence: The package's name as its manager spells it. It is also this object's native name on dpkg and rpm; on Nix the native name is the name-version the store publishes, and this is the half of it before the version.

Version.sentence: The installed version, printed exactly as the manager reports it — a Debian epoch, an Ubuntu revision and a Nix suffix all travel unparsed, because comparing versions is the manager's job and mangling them into a common shape would lose the only string an operator can match against an advisory.

Manager.sentence: Which package manager answered. It rides every row so the answer names its own provenance: one question, asked the same way on every host, and the row says who is speaking rather than leaving a reader to infer it from the operating system.

Architecture.sentence: The architecture the package was built for, as dpkg and rpm report it — `all`/`noarch` for the ones that are architecture-independent. Nix has no such field, and a row from the store carries no architecture rather than an invented one.

StorePath.sentence: The /nix/store path this package is linked into the system environment from. The hash is content-addressed, so the same path on two machines is the same build; dpkg and rpm have no store, and their rows carry no such fact.

collections.redaction_exemption: neither package database has a credential surface: every value served is a package name, a version string, an architecture token or a store path, and dpkg-query and rpm are asked for exactly those fields by a format string this collector supplies. The identifiers published verbatim are archive-wide constants — the same strings on every machine that installed the same thing — which is what makes them safe to publish and useful to compare. The bound is stated because it is a decision and not a shape: a locally built package carries a name somebody in this estate chose, and a capture holding one would need that name classified as content rather than exempted here.
